evidence_quote: These districts already offered voluntary summer learning programs to low-income and low-achieving elementary school students and were willing to adopt common programming elements and participate in a randomized controlled trial for two summers.
resolved_title: Learning from Summer: Effects of Voluntary Summer Learning Programs on Low-Income Urban Youth
notes: National Summer Learning Project: the Wallace Foundation selected five urban districts serving low-income students; students applied and were randomized (opt_in 1). Student eligibility criteria were set by each district and are described in McCombs et al. (2014), not here (p. 31); students mandated to summer school for poor grades or retention risk were excluded (p. 31), and the share at the lowest state proficiency level ranged from 12 to 81 percent by district (p. 32). Level coded school because the student rules are not stated in this source; both is possible. Kraft n 4,484 to 4,505 fits 5,639 randomized applicants less attrition.

evidence_quote: We conducted the study in three large urban school districts–one in the northeast, one in the midwest, and one in the south – each of which had a superintendent or technology director interested in evaluating the CAI program already in use in their district.
resolved_title: Technology's Edge: The Educational Benefits of Computer-Aided Instruction
notes: NBER w14240 text of the 2009 AEJ Economic Policy article. Pre-algebra and algebra classes in 17 schools were randomized within period pools; no student rule beyond class enrollment. Kraft n 1,605 matches the sample with both pre and post NWEA tests.

evidence_quote: The research design incorporated same-classroom pretest-matched controls in which one-half of each class used the ILS for mathematics while the other half used it for reading.
resolved_title: Mindless or mindful use of integrated learning systems
notes: Book chapter; two elementary schools; within-class matched design, not a lottery. No eligibility rule beyond class membership stated in the publisher abstract. Kraft n 360 to 400 cannot be checked from the abstract.

evidence_quote: The participants are 49 first-grade through fifth-grade classrooms from predominantly minority and poor contexts across the nation.

Data flag: Kraft n 613 matches neither the abstract's 49 classrooms nor the WWC's 1,099 students in 57 classrooms or 855 in grades 1 to 3; probably an analytic sample.

evidence_quote: The participating teachers used the program in their randomly selected "CT" classes for six months during the 2005-2006 school year while teaching their other classes with their standard materials. The experiment involved nine teachers, 22 classes, and 541 students.

evidence_quote: It focused on school districts that had low student achievement and large proportions of students in poverty, but these were general guidelines rather than strict eligibility criteria.

Districts were recruited with a stated focus on low achievement and poverty, but the report calls this a guideline rather than a criterion and vendors suggested many districts, so a reviewer may prefer universal; all students in participating classrooms were tested. evidence_quote: staff in the assessment department at OSPI, who determined that a score of 390 or below on the Washington Assessment of Student Learning (WASL, the state reading assessment at the time) was roughly equivalent to two years below grade level. Kraft n 295 to 759 by grade fits the Year 1 grade 6 and grade 8 samples.

evidence_quote: Participating in the experiment were a (final) total of 92 elementary teachers in grades three to five, who were recruited from public schools in three locations: Miami-Dade County (Florida), Richland Two (South Carolina), and Buffalo (New York). evidence_quote: Students in Grades 7–10 are eligible for the targeted intervention if they are reading at least 2 years below grade level as measured by their total reading score on the OAKS or the Degrees of Reading Power (for Grade 10 selection only) administered the previous spring.

notes: Nine Portland schools were eligible because all received Title I funding, had missed AYP, and had many students two or more years behind (p. 9); students were then screened on OAKS or DRP (p. 41). Kraft's five effects with n 822 to 1,776 and grades 7-8 look like middle-school subsamples pooled across years (Years 1 to 4 randomized 1,311, 443, 684, and 457 students), hence mixed_samples 1. The text file concatenates the Year 5 and Year 4 reports.

evidence_quote: The study was conducted in three schools, involving 14 teachers and 859 students. resolved_title: Impact of the National Writing Project's College-Ready Writers Program in High-Need Rural Districts

notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: first page names Guryan, Kim, and Park (NBER w20918, January 2015), the working-paper version of Guryan, Kim, and Park 2016, Economics of Education Review, which the BEE summer-programs synthesis lists as Guryan et al. evidence_quote: We worked with HMH to recruit 12 schools with grades 3, 4, and 5. We randomized intact grade-level teams that volunteered for participation to the MIF and control groups.
resolved_title: Assessing Impacts of Math in Focus, a 'Singapore Math' Program for American Schools
notes: SREE 2015 abstract (ED562089) of the 2016 JREE article; one urban Nevada district. Grade-level teams volunteered (tie-breaker 6); no student rule. Kraft n 1,641 is an analytic sample of the 2,235 rostered students. Data flags: Kraft's grade span 3-5,9-12 is wrong (grades 3 to 5 only), and the WWC row attached to 432 is Newman et al. (Alabama AMSTI), a different study.

evidence_quote: Subjects for this study were third, fourth, and fifth grade students in the Derry Township School District in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Derry Township is a small district with approximately 2,500 students in a wealthy community where the average I.Q. is 118.

notes: The district was chosen to study high achievers ('a district where achievement is already above average', p. 1), so selection on a characteristic at the district level; all students in 12 classrooms, no student rule. Students were randomly assigned to classrooms and two classes per grade were taught with TAI, not a lottery on treatment. Data flags: the article reports 247 students (34 and 35, 44 and 44, 46 and 44 across grades 3 to 5), not Kraft's n 588, and Kraft's grade span 3-12 is wrong (grades 3 to 5). Children were pretested in school and randomized; 'voluntary' describes the summer reading, not enrollment. Data flag: Kraft lists the subject as Math with n 317; the outcomes are reading comprehension and vocabulary (370 randomized).

resolved_title: Scaffolding Voluntary Summer Reading for Children in Grades 3 to 5: An Experimental Study
notes: No eligibility rule stated. Kraft n 400 matches.

resolved_title: Effects of a Voluntary Summer Reading Intervention on Reading Achievement: Results From a Randomized Field Trial

evidence_quote: In this randomized controlled trial involving 312 students enrolled in an after-school program, the authors generated intention-to-treat and treatment-on-the-treated estimates of the program’s impact on several literacy outcomes of fourth, fifth, and sixth graders reading below proficiency on a state assessment at baseline.
resolved_title: Can a Mixed-Method Literacy Intervention Improve the Reading Achievement of Low-Performing Elementary School Students in an After-School Program? Results From a Randomized Controlled Trial of READ 180 Enterprise
notes: Twin of 482-kim-2010 (same trial, Reading and Writing 2010 article). Data flags: the WWC row attached to 483 is the Pathway Project (Kim, Olson, et al. 2011, Santa Ana English learners), which belongs to 485-olson-2012, not this READ 180 study; the codebook's worked example for key 483-kim-2011 describes that Pathway sample and so applies to 485. evidence_quote: The sample included 2,726 English learner students in grades 6 to 12. All students were English learners, 95% of students were Hispanic, and Spanish was the first language for 88% of students.
resolved_title: Enhancing the Interpretive Reading and Analytical Writing of Mainstreamed English Learners in Secondary School
notes: The abstract (title and text: mainstreamed English learners, 72 Santa Ana teachers randomized) and the WWC sample text agree, so confidence medium rather than low. Kraft n 4,459 is plausible for the two-year sample; the WWC-reviewed sample is 2,726. Kraft's 0.48 is the on-demand writing assessment and 0.10 the standardized writing test.

evidence_quote: This study examined the efficacy of a supplemental, multicomponent adolescent reading intervention for middle school students who scored below proficient on a state literacy assessment.

All eight schools were Title I but no school selection rule is stated, so level student. Kraft n 398 is an analytic sample of 483.

evidence_quote: We use data from a large-scale, school-level randomized experiment conducted in 2010-2011 in public schools in Indiana. Our sample includes more than 30,000 students in 70 schools.
resolved_title: Effects of Interim Assessments on Student Achievement: Evidence From a Large-Scale Experiment (Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 2016)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (ERIC EJ1115334, DOI 10.1080/19345747.2015.1116031) is the correct article, Konstantopoulos, Li, Miller, and van der Ploeg 2016; no open full text was found. Seventy Indiana public schools were randomized to interim assessment programs (mCLASS in K-2, Acuity in 3-8) serving all students in the school, and the abstract states no need-based rule for schools; coded universal on the Festas precedent in codebook section 6, with medium confidence because the abstract does not say how the 70 schools were recruited. Kraft's n 13,944 is presumably the grade 3-8 Acuity math sample; Kraft's grades_all K-6 differs from the abstract's K-8.

evidence_quote: The study was conducted in one school district and involved 76 teachers and their classes in grades 3 to 6. Within each grade level, half the teachers were randomly assigned to the treatment group and half were randomly assigned to the control group.

notes: Writing outcome (6+1 Trait), listed by Kraft under reading. No selection rule for the district or students is stated; low-poverty sample (10 percent FRPL, under 1 percent ELL or minority). Kraft n 1,592 matches the students with complete data.
